title: Best AI Video Translation Tools in 2026
summary: A practical comparison of nine AI video translation tools for customer education and product marketing teams.
body_markdown:
Localizing a training library, a product demo, or an onboarding series for international customers usually comes down to one early decision: translate the captions, or replace the voice entirely. That choice determines cost, turnaround time, and which vendor actually fits the job, long before any feature comparison matters. This guide breaks down nine AI video translation tools, including Clueso so customer education and product marketing teams can match the right tool to the right video.


## Subtitles or dubbing: the decision that determines your shortlist


Your audience’s viewing habits should determine whether you translate subtitles or replace the spoken audio. Subtitle translation works well when viewers can watch the screen and read along. Full dubbing fits videos that people may hear without closely watching, including sales enablement content and customer-facing launch videos.


Subtitle translation converts captions into another language while preserving the original voice track. The workflow avoids translated voice generation and lip synchronization, so each additional language usually requires less production work. Customer education teams can use subtitles for self-serve help videos and in-app product tutorials where the screen demonstrates each action. Reviewers can also inspect product terminology in written form and correct mistranslated interface labels before publishing.


Full dubbing replaces the narration with translated speech. Some video translation software can preserve the speaker’s vocal character or synchronize translated speech with visible mouth movements. Those steps add processing and review work, especially when a video includes several speakers or tightly timed dialogue. Product marketing teams may accept the added cost for polished demos and launch campaigns aimed at international markets.


The source video should narrow your shortlist further. A screen recording depends mainly on clear narration, readable captions, and accurate timing around product actions.[Clueso](https://www.clueso.io/) fits that format because its workflow starts with a raw screen recording and turns it into polished customer education or product demo content. A separate dubbing specialist may fit better when you already have a produced presenter video and need convincing lip synchronization across languages.


Choose the delivery format before comparing vendor feature lists. Subtitles suit content that viewers watch closely, while dubbing suits content that must remain understandable when viewers rely on the audio.


## Clueso


**What it is:** Clueso turns raw screen recordings into polished product videos with enhanced scripts, AI voiceovers, automatic zooms, captions, and reusable branded structures. You can translate captions or subtitles while leaving the original audio track unchanged. Viewers hear the source-language narration and read localized text, which avoids producing a separate dubbed track for every market.


Clueso keeps translation inside the workflow used to create the original video. You can record a product walkthrough, polish the script and visuals, and produce localized versions without exporting a finished video into separate video translation software. That approach suits help centers with dozens or hundreds of screen-based videos, especially when each product update creates another localization task.


**Best for** :[Clueso](https://www.clueso.io/) fits customer education and product marketing teams that create videos from screen recordings. Common examples include self-serve help videos, in-app tutorials, customer onboarding, product launch demos, and sales enablement content for international markets.


**Pros** Subtitle translation controls costs because each language version reuses the original narration. Clueso also reduces editing work before translation by improving the spoken script and generating captions from the recording. For videos that need localized narration, its language-conversion and AI voiceover features support multilingual production without requiring voice actors.


Reusable Clueprints help customer-facing videos follow the same branding and structure across languages. Clueso can also patch an affected clip when the product interface changes, which reduces the work required to update localized tutorials. Updated videos propagate wherever you have embedded or linked them.


**Cons** Clueso does not target lip-synced dubbing for face-on-camera marketing, entertainment, or highly produced brand campaigns. HeyGen and other dubbing-first tools fit better when translated mouth movements and presenter realism drive the buying decision.


**Pricing** Clueso offers a free plan. Its Solo plan costs $40 per month when billed annually, while enterprise pricing depends on usage and organizational requirements. The subscription covers the broader screen-recording-to-video workflow rather than charging only for standalone subtitle translation.


## HappyScribe


**What it is:** HappyScribe transcribes video, translates transcripts and subtitles, and provides a timeline editor for correcting wording and timing. You can export common caption formats or send finished captions to YouTube and Vimeo. Human linguists can review AI translations for terminology, cultural nuance, and readability.


**Best for:** HappyScribe fits customer education and product marketing teams that need polished subtitles for finished videos without a screen-recording production workflow.


**Pros** Human review gives you more control over customer-facing language than an AI-only workflow. HappyScribe also supports a wide range of subtitle formats and integrations. Reported translation coverage varies by product page, with roughly 60 to 80 or more languages and human services covering over 65 language pairs.


**Cons** HappyScribe does not provide full AI dubbing, voice cloning, or lip sync. Product marketers who need localized narration for launch demos or sales videos should choose a dubbing-first tool. HappyScribe also requires you to import a finished video rather than helping create it from a screen recording.


**Pricing** Independent pricing research lists Basic at $17 per month, Pro at $29, and Business at $89, with included AI minutes varying by tier. Human subtitling and proofreading start near $2 per minute. Buyers should confirm current prices and language coverage before purchasing.


## Smartcat


**What it is:** Smartcat combines video translation with a broader enterprise localization platform. One workflow handles transcription, subtitle translation, dubbing, voice cloning, editing, and export.


**Best for:** Smartcat suits large customer education and product marketing groups that localize onboarding videos, product demos, and sales enablement content across many markets.


**Pros.** Smartcat supports subtitles and dubbing across more than 280 languages. Its subtitle editor provides timing controls and live previews, while its dubbing tools let you adjust voices and scripts. Large localization groups can also hire reviewers through Smartcat’s marketplace, which includes more than 500,000 reviewers. That human QA option helps when customer-facing terminology needs careful review.


**Cons.** Smartcat serves broader localization programs rather than video production alone, so smaller product teams may find it heavier than a dedicated video tool. Fast speech, strong accents, and background noise can reduce accuracy. Dubbed voices may also need manual edits before publication.


**Pricing.** Smartcat does not publish standard video translation prices. Buyers need to request pricing based on their localization volume and workflow requirements.


## HeyGen


**What it is:** HeyGen combines AI dubbing, voice cloning, and lip synchronization. Its mobile Translate app offers video dubbing with regenerated mouth movements and simpler audio dubbing that leaves the visuals unchanged. HeyGen claims support for more than 175 languages, and users can add translated captions to dubbed videos.


**Best for:** HeyGen suits product marketing teams that need translated speakers to look and sound natural in launch videos, sales content, and face-on-camera demos.


**Pros** Lip synchronization makes HeyGen a strong option when customers watch the speaker rather than a product screen. Voice cloning preserves the original speaker’s vocal character across languages, while audio-only dubbing provides a faster alternative when matched mouth movements add little value.


**Cons** HeyGen fits produced, presenter-led video better than screen-recorded tutorials. A 2023 hands-on test found that lip-synced dubbing worked best with one front-facing speaker. HeyGen now promotes speaker recognition for multi-person conversations, but buyers should test their own footage before committing a large library. Mobile credits can also be difficult to forecast because the app does not show a fixed credit cost for each video.


**Pricing** Mobile pricing includes $10 weekly and $29 monthly plans with 70 credits, plus a $279 annual plan and one-time credit packs. Web and enterprise costs may differ, so larger customer education libraries need a direct quote.


## Rask AI


**What it is:** Rask AI automates dubbing and caption translation across more than 130 languages. The platform supports voice cloning, multi-speaker dubbing, lip sync, and downloadable captions. It works well for finished onboarding videos, product demos, and sales enablement content that needs distribution across several markets.


**Best for:** Customer education and product marketing teams that localize large video libraries through an API or follow a steady release calendar.


**Pros** Broad language coverage and API support make Rask suitable for high-volume localization. Teams can choose translated captions or dubbed audio, and roughly 32 languages support voice cloning.


**Cons** Rask focuses narrowly on video and audio localization. It does not generate help articles or documentation from the source video. Independent testing also reports that its lip sync trails HeyGen and Synthesia, particularly when footage includes complex audio or multiple speakers.


**Pricing** Plans start at $60 per month, or $33 per month when billed annually with 300 minutes per year. Rask charges minutes for each target language, so a five-minute video translated into three languages consumes 15 minutes. Enhanced lip sync consumes three credits per video minute, and lower plans cannot purchase overages.


## Vozo


**What it is:** Vozo localizes finished videos into more than 160 languages and dialects. Its subtitle mode produces translated or bilingual captions, while its dubbing modes offer two voice approaches. VoiceREAL clones the original speaker’s delivery. VoiceNATIVE uses a native-accent voice for the target market, which can suit customer onboarding videos and localized product demos.


**Best for** : Product marketing and customer education teams that need subtitles, dubbing, lip sync, and translated on-screen graphics in one tool.


**Pros**


Visual Translate detects and replaces text in overlays, slides, and other graphics while preserving the original layout and styling. Product marketers can localize a launch video without manually rebuilding every title card. Vozo also supports optional lip sync, terminology glossaries, subtitle file uploads, and line-level editing with regenerated audio.


**Cons**


Vozo works with imported finished videos rather than building customer education content directly from a screen recording. Product teams that produce frequent software walkthroughs may prefer Clueso’s screen-recording-to-video workflow. Vozo’s broad feature set may also exceed the needs of teams that only want translated captions.


**Pricing**


Vozo offers three free projects and paid plans for further use, but the available product materials do not provide exact tier prices. Enterprise buyers can contact sales for workspace, security, support, and API options.


## Kapwing


**What it is:** Kapwing combines browser-based video editing with automatic captions, subtitle translation, AI dubbing, voice cloning, and lip sync. Its translation and dubbing tools support more than 70 languages.


**Best for:** Customer education and product marketing teams that already edit help center videos, product demos, and launch content in Kapwing.


**Pros** You can translate a product video and adjust its timeline, text overlays, audio, and branding in one editor. Kapwing supports subtitle-only localization and full dubbing, which lets you choose a lower-cost option for help content or dubbed audio for customer-facing campaigns.


**Cons** Translation sits inside a broad editing suite rather than a dedicated localization workflow. Teams managing large multilingual customer education libraries may need stronger terminology controls, review routing, and translation management elsewhere.


**Pricing** Kapwing charges per user each month. The Free plan includes 10 minutes of automatic subtitles, while Pro costs $16 and raises that allowance to 300 minutes. Video translation becomes available on the $50 Business plan, which includes up to 900 translation minutes and 900 automatic subtitle minutes per month. Enterprise pricing uses custom allowances.


## Veed


**What it is:** Veed is a browser-based video editor with subtitle translation and AI dubbing inside a broader editing workflow. It supports 125+ subtitle languages, AI voice translation, voice preservation, and optional lip sync. Veed does not publish a clear count for dubbing languages.


**Best for:** Customer education and product marketing teams that already edit launch demos, onboarding videos, and social clips in Veed.


**Pros.** You can generate, translate, style, and edit subtitles without transferring files to separate localization software. Its templates and visual editing tools suit product demos, promotional clips, and customer education content for global channels.


**Cons.** Veed reserves SRT controls and proofreading for Enterprise. Customer education teams may find that restriction difficult when reviewers need to verify product terminology or reuse caption files. An independent comparison rates its multilingual localization workflow as limited, so complex global launches and large multilingual video libraries may need a dedicated localization platform.


**Pricing.** Current translation and dubbing rates are not available in the supplied research. Ask Veed which plan includes your required dubbing languages, translation allowances, SRT export, and proofreading.

## Which approach fits your team


Choose subtitle translation for large customer education libraries with tight budgets and frequent product updates. Subtitles preserve the original voice track, while reviewers can check product names and technical terms before publishing. This approach fits self-serve help centers, in-app tutorials, and onboarding videos where viewers can read along.


Choose full dubbing when customers need to understand the video without reading the screen. Localized voice tracks fit product launch demos, sales enablement content, and marketing videos that viewers may play while multitasking. Dubbing costs more because each language requires voice generation and audio review. Lip-synced video adds another production step when a presenter appears on camera.


Choose[Clueso](https://www.clueso.io/) when your customer education or product demo starts as a screen recording. Clueso turns the recording into a polished video, then lets you translate captions without replacing the original audio when dubbing adds little value. You can keep one production workflow for multilingual walkthroughs instead of moving finished videos into a separate translation tool. A dubbing specialist fits better when you need localized speech and precise lip sync for presenter-led marketing content.


Your source-video format and the way customers consume the finished video should determine the tool.


## FAQs


**How much more does dubbing cost than subtitle translation?**


Dubbing usually costs more because the software must generate a new voice track and may synchronize speech with the speaker’s mouth. Costs often increase for every target language and each minute of video. Subtitle translation changes text while leaving the audio and video untouched, which makes it better suited to large customer education libraries with limited budgets.


**Does subtitle translation preserve the original voiceover?**


Yes. Subtitle translation adds translated captions while keeping the original voice track. Viewers hear the source language and read the translation, which works well for help center videos, product tutorials, and technical demos where precise terminology matters more than localized audio.


**What does language pair coverage mean?**


A language pair combines one source language with one target language, such as English to Japanese. A vendor’s total language count does not guarantee support for every possible pair or feature. Dubbing, voice cloning, transcription, and subtitles may each support different language sets, so confirm the exact pair and output type you need.


**How should you manage customer education videos that change often?**


Keep scripts and approved terminology in a controlled source, then review translated captions whenever product behavior or regulated claims change. Clueso can monitor product code for changes, recommend updates, patch affected video segments, and propagate the revised video wherever it is embedded. A qualified reviewer should still verify legal, safety, or compliance-sensitive wording before publication.
